title: Kali's one small opening
hookLine: Kali arrives too late for the swayamvara, waits for one small lapse, and enters Nala
carry: shaucha, small purity, guards the heart

cards: On their way home from the wedding, the gods meet latecomers on the road. One is Kali, the spirit of strife and bad luck, with his companion Dvapara. Kali is hurrying to the swayamvara to win Damayanti.

The gods tell him he's missed it: she has chosen Nala. Kali doesn't take it well. He swears to get into Nala, to take his kingdom, to part him from his wife, and he tells Dvapara to get into the dice.
Then he does something quietly frightening. He waits.

teach.b: Nala, the story says, is a good king. He rules well, offers sacrifices, loves Damayanti, and they have children. Kali can't find a way in.
So he waits, a long, long time. Then one evening Nala relieves himself and, before sitting down to his evening prayers, forgets to wash his feet. That's all: one small lapse in a careful life.
Kali goes to Nala's brother, Pushkara, and whispers: challenge Nala at dice. Nala, with Kali inside him, can't say no. He loses, and loses again.
His ministers come to stop him; Damayanti herself comes. He won't even look up. So she does the one thing in her power: she has the charioteer, Varshneya, take their children to her father's house.
Then Pushkara asks for one more stake: Damayanti. Nala won't do it. He walks out of his own city in a single cloth, and Damayanti walks after him.
Now the teaching, and it starts with the feet.

Washing hands and feet before worship is ordinary Hindu life; you'll see it at temple doors and home shrines. The tradition calls this purity shaucha, and the Yoga Sutras name it first among the daily observances.
Many teachers read Nala's story this way: trouble rarely storms in; it waits for one small lapse of attention. And the name fits: tradition calls our own age the Kali Yuga, the age of strife.
For today: those small acts before prayer aren't fussiness. They're how you arrive awake.

how: In the Mahabharata's telling, the sage Brihadashva narrates Nala's loss at dice to Yudhishthira; in that telling, Kali gets in through a small ritual lapse, feet left unwashed before the evening rite.

o: the spirit of strife who waits for a single lapse
the charioteer who carries the children to safety
the brother who challenges Nala to a dice game

games.q: the game that won't stop — tap the pairs.
p: waits for a lapse, then enters Nala

s: Nala staked Damayanti and lost her
when Pushkara asked for her, Nala refused and walked out with a single cloth.
Kali entered Nala through a small lapse
Nala forgot to wash his feet before his evening prayers, and Kali entered him.
washing before worship is a real Hindu practice, part of shaucha
purity, which the Yoga Sutras name first among the daily observances; Nala's skipped washing is where Kali got in.

games.q: you're tired and want to skip washing before your evening prayer, just this once. by Nala's story, what fits?
o: skip it; God doesn't care about feet.
wash anyway: shaucha is how you arrive attentive, and in Nala's story one small lapse was all Kali needed.
skip the prayer too, since you're not clean.
games.why: Kali waited years for Nala's one lapse. many teachers read it as: trouble waits at small cracks, and small purity keeps you awake.

practice: If you can, wash your hands, or your hands and feet, before you sit, the way many Hindus do before worship. Sit and feel the coolness fade from your skin. Breathe in, and arrive; breathe out, and let the day's dust go.
If you pray, begin with Om, or Om Namah Shivaya, or your own words; if not, simply rest, clean and awake.

wordCard.voice: Kali. The spirit of strife who waits years for one small opening, a forgotten washing, before he enters a good king and will not let the dice stop.

orig.note: Sanskrit Kali (with short vowels), the spirit of strife and bad luck in this story, not the goddess Kālī.

carryVoice: Your line: shaucha, small purity, guards the heart. In Nala's story, one forgotten washing opened a door. Day seven hundred ninety, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Nalopakhyana: Kali and Dvapara meet the gods; Kali enters Nala; Pushkara's dice game; the children sent away; Nala leaves the city)
Yoga Sutras 2.32 (shaucha first among the niyamas); washing hands and feet before worship; the Kali Yuga as the present age in Hindu cosmology
